query: Why are some incidents resolved inefficiently, and which underlying issues drive it?

per_column.name: resolution_time_hours
per_column.rationale: Directly central to diagnosing inefficient resolution; a strong new axis derived from opened_at/closed_at. However, the row samples show closed_at == sys_updated_on and no opened_at is exposed, yet nonzero values like 161.13 are produced -- the derivation is opaque and the heavy spike at exactly 24 (57 rows) is suspicious, suggesting a default/fallback rather than a true reading of the timestamps. Partially grounded but with signs of unwarranted specifics.

per_column.name: is_reassigned
per_column.rationale: Reassignment is a plausible driver of inefficiency and a useful grouping variable. But the table has no reassignment_count or work-notes field; assignment_group/assigned_to alone do not reveal reassignment history. A 79% reassigned rate asserted with no supporting evidence field looks largely invented.

per_column.name: expected_resolution_hours
per_column.rationale: A baseline/SLA expectation is exactly what an efficiency analysis needs. But values appear to be priority/category-derived constants (e.g. 181.8 repeated 336 times) that are model assumptions, not stated SLAs present in the source. Defensible as a warranted heuristic yet not truly grounded in table content.

per_column.name: resolution_delay_hours
per_column.rationale: The gap between actual and expected is the core quantity for the query. Groundedness inherits the weaknesses of its two inputs (resolution_time and the assumed expected baseline), so its specifics rest partly on invented expectations.

per_column.name: inefficiency_flag
per_column.rationale: A clean binary segment for the query's central 'inefficient vs not' comparison. It is a deterministic function of the delay column, so its correctness follows from those inputs; the thresholding itself is a reasonable derived judgment.

per_column.name: inefficiency_drivers
per_column.rationale: Most directly answers 'which underlying issues drive it' by naming drivers per row -- high leverage. But it composes the reassigned flag (unsupported) and pct-above-expected (against an assumed baseline), so the specific driver tags carry the same groundedness concerns; the labels themselves are sound restatements of the computed inputs.

judge.rationale: Every added column is squarely aimed at the query -- they give distinct, combinable axes (duration, expectation, delay, a binary segment, and named drivers) with little redundancy, so analytical usefulness is high. Groundedness is the weak point: the exposed source rows show only closed_at/sys_updated_on (identical) and no opened_at, no SLA field, and no reassignment history, yet the operator confidently produces nonzero resolution times, constant 'expected' baselines, and a 79% reassigned rate. These are plausible heuristics but assert specifics the visible table does not clearly support, and the exact-24 and repeated-181.8 spikes suggest fallback constants presented as measured values.
